newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition plan more poll protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition plan more poll protests.

text.p: Serbia's opposition planned more protests on Friday, hoping to force authorities to block President Slobodan Milosevic's attempt to annul election results which went badly against him.

Thousands marched through Belgrade and towns across Serbia on Thursday to demand that the results of local polls held last Sunday be recognised. The opposition said it expected electoral commissions and courts to give their final rulings on Friday.

Leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition accuse the government of extensive fraud by annulling votes which gave the opposition sweeping victories in 15 of the 18 biggest towns in Serbia.

Milosevic's ruling Socialists conceded defeat in Belgrade and the northern town of Novi Sad, but in the industrial town of Nis turned a major defeat into victory after the local election commission ruled in their favour.
Some 20,000 people marched through Belgrade on Thursday, waving opposition party flags and flinging insults at Milosevic, in the biggest demonstrations to hit the capital for three years.
It was the fourth day of protests since the opposition claimed victory in the run-off municipal elections.
Zoran Djindjic, one of three opposition coalition leaders expected to become the new mayor of Belgrade, said protests would continue until the Socialists verified the poll results.
Main demonstrations are scheduled in Belgrade at 1400 gmt on Friday, after working hours. The influential student organisation is expected to join at noon, according to opposition sources.
The unrest is bad news for Milosevic, already under scrutiny in the West for his handling of domestic affairs.
Students last took to the streets in the wake of March 9, 1991 demonstrations which Milosevic crushed with massive police force and tanks. Two men were killed.
The students then staged a round-the-clock sit-in in the centre of Belgrade, forcing him to make concessions.

Police have so far shown great restraint in Belgrade but not in Nis, where they were deployed in force against protests. Any move against students in the capital was bound to provoke disgruntled workers in Belgrade's vast industry, diplomats said.

"The tenacity and endurance of the demonstrations is sorely testing the authorities. The most alarming fact for them is that the numbers of demonstrators in Belgrade is growing instead of diminishing," one said.

Milosevic has already been warned by the United States to improve his poor human rights record if he wants to see lifted an "outer wall" of sanctions which bars Belgrade from desperately-needed foreign capital.
The United States and Britain have voiced grave concerns over the opposition's allegations. The European Union is expected to issue a joint statement in Brussels on Friday.

Milosevic's left coalition won federal elections two weeks ago, mainly thanks to his new image as a peace-maker indispensable to the West for helping implement the peace process in Bosnia and restoring stability in the Balkans.
"That image will be hard to defend if the opposition's allegations prove correct and he pursues the current hardline course," a veteran western observer said.
